articles.title: Homem é detido suspeito de pôr fogo próximo a UTI com crianças em MT | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo a Guarda Municipal, fogo atingiu tubulações da unidade de saúde e a fumaça entrou na UTI. Hospital afirma que não houve danos à estrutura ou prejuízo ao atendimento.
articles.summary: Segundo a Guarda Municipal, fogo atingiu tubulações da unidade de saúde e a fumaça entrou na UTI. Hospital afirma que não houve danos à estrutura ou prejuízo ao atendimento.
articles.body:
Um homem identificado como Maikon Silva de Moraes, de 37 anos, foi detido nesta quarta-feira (26), suspeito de pôr fogo em um local próximo à Unidade de Terapia Intensiva (UTI) e à maternidade do Pronto-Socorro Municipal de Várzea Grande , região metropolitana de Cuiabá. Segundo a Guarda Municipal, a fumaça entrou na área da UTI, onde havia seis crianças recebendo atendimento médico.

Imagens registradas por funcionários da unidade foram disponibilizadas aos agentes da Guarda Municipal e auxiliaram na identificação do suspeito. O vídeo mostra o local onde o fogo teria sido provocado (assista acima) .

Homem identificado como Maikon Silva de Moraes, de 37 anos, foi detido nesta quarta-feira (26), suspeito de pôr fogo em um local próximo à UTI e à maternidade de Várzea Grande — Foto: Guarda Municipal de Várzea Grande

De acordo com a Guarda Municipal, o fogo atingiu tubulações e derreteu parte do encanamento. A fumaça também teria chegado à parte interna da unidade de saúde.

A direção do Hospital e Pronto-Socorro de Várzea Grande, no entanto, informou que o fogo não comprometeu a estrutura do hospital, os equipamentos ou o atendimento aos pacientes. Segundo a unidade, não houve danos elétricos, prejuízos estruturais ou intercorrências com os bebês internados.

Ainda conforme o hospital, servidores identificaram as chamas, acionaram a Guarda Municipal e apagaram o fogo que atingia papelões na área externa.

Segundo a Guarda Municipal, Maikon teria sido localizado próximo ao local onde o fogo foi provocado e detido a partir das imagens fornecidas pela equipe do hospital. Ele negou ter ateado fogo e não explicou aos agentes o motivo da ação.

Segundo o relato dos agentes, ele também teria tentado avançar contra a equipe durante a abordagem. O suspeito apresentava uma pequena escoriação no lado direito do rosto e foi encaminhado para atendimento médico antes de ser levado à Central de Flagrantes. Maikon deve responder pelos crimes de incêndio e dano ao patrimônio público .

A ocorrência foi registrada após um chamado feito pelo Centro de Inteligência Municipal de Segurança, pelo telefone 153, a pedido da coordenação da unidade de saúde. O Corpo de Bombeiros não foi acionado.

articles.title: Idosos são retirados de casa de repouso interditada parcialmente em São Bernardo do Campo | G1
articles.standfirst: Famílias retiraram nesta quarta-feira (26) os idosos que ainda estavam no local, onde a Vigilância Sanitária encontrou remédios vencidos, falhas no registro de medicamentos e problemas na estrutura.
articles.summary: Famílias retiraram nesta quarta-feira (26) os idosos que ainda estavam no local, onde a Vigilância Sanitária encontrou remédios vencidos, falhas no registro de medicamentos e problemas na estrutura.
articles.body:
Os sete idosos que ainda estavam na casa de repouso em São Bernardo de Campo, que foi interditada parcialmente pela Vigilância Sanitária na segunda-feira (24 ), foram retirados pelas famílias na tarde desta quarta-feira (26).

No abrigo, os fiscais encontraram remédios vencidos, falhas no registro da medicação e problemas no controle de remédios de uso restrito. Também foram identificados problemas na estrutura física, que, segundo a Vigilância, não estava adequada para este serviço.

Funcionários contam que os donos e responsáveis pela casa, que são marido e mulher, se desentenderam e abandonaram o local. Quem ficou na linha de frente, como o técnico em enfermagem João Paulo Leite Pereira, passou a lidar com diferentes problemas.

Depois de uma denúncia, o que já era relatado por funcionários e familiares apareceu no laudo de uma vistoria da Vigilância Sanitária.

Por causa das irregularidades, o órgão determinou a interdição parcial da instituição. Com a decisão, novos idosos não podem ser acolhidos.

Os proprietários da casa de repouso disseram que sabem que a instituição não pode receber novos pacientes, mas não falaram nada sobre o que será feito no local.

Logically speaking, it makes sense to store things in the room where you use them. Bathrooms are the rare exception. That's right, your steamy showers do more than just fog up a mirror; they can damage makeup, medication and other everyday essentials.

Heat and humidity are the chief culprits here. It's how you end up with tarnished jewelry, oxidized serums and mold growth on retainers, among other things. This doesn't mean you have to clear out your bathroom and put everything elsewhere. Nope, I rallied a group of experts — a cosmetic chemist, dentist, orthodontist and jeweler — to nail down a list of the products that are most at risk. Here's what the pros say should be removed from your bathroom pronto (and where you should store them instead).

Medicine cabinets belong in the bathroom, but that doesn't mean your medication belongs in them. Sounds pretty contradictory, doesn't it? Blame heat, humidity and moisture, which create a perfect storm, according to Kelly Dobos , a cosmetic chemist at the University of Cincinnati.

"Bathrooms experience frequent fluctuations in temperature and humidity from showers and baths, and those conditions can accelerate the degradation of some active ingredients over time," she says. Over time, moisture can also cause tablets and capsules to "soften, swell, or break down before their expiration date."

Vitamins and supplements aren't quite as sensitive, but Dobos warns that "excessive heat and humidity can still reduce potency or affect physical quality, particularly for products in tablet, capsule, or gummy form."

A cool, dry spot in your house, such as a dresser drawer or linen closet, is your best bet. "Always be sure to follow any specific storage instructions on the package, as some medications require refrigeration or special handling," Dobos adds.

Divvy up your daily medications and supplements into these daily containers, then pop each one out of the larger organizer so you can take just what you need when you're away from home. Each container — which holds six fish oil pills, nine capsules, eight vitamins and 18 round pills — is divided into two, making it easy to keep morning and night medications separate.

Getting ready in front of your bathroom mirror is one thing; storing your makeup in your bathroom is another. "While cosmetics are formulated to be reasonably robust under normal conditions, repeated exposure to steam and warm temperatures can gradually affect texture, stability, fragrance and preservative performance," Dobos says, adding that humidity may "increase the risk of contamination" each time a product is opened and used.

Liquid-based products — namely, foundation, concealer and mascara — pose the highest risks, whereas pressed powder, blush, bronzer, eye shadow and lipstick "tend to be more stable because they contain little or no water."

Keep your makeup collection away from heat, humidity and direct sunlight. Dobos recommends carving out a spot "in a bedroom vanity drawer or cabinet," but a tabletop organizer will do the trick if needed.

Lacking drawer space? Keep all of your makeup products contained in this two-drawer organizer, which lets you stand foundations, setting sprays and fragrances upright. It also keeps lipsticks, eye makeup and other smaller staples out of sight (but not out of mind).

Your skin care products need a little TLC too. Yep, retinol and vitamin C can be a bit finicky, so you're better off storing them outside the bathroom to help keep their formulas as potent as possible. According to Julie Pefferman, cosmetic chemist and founder of Cosmeta , a change in color can be a sign of oxidation. "Discoloration is the first thing you will see," she says. "However, just because it goes brown (from clear or pale yellow) doesn't mean it's fully oxidized; it just won't be fully potent."

The right packaging is key here. Look for opaque bottles, airless pumps or aluminum tubes when shopping for vitamin C serums, since Dobos says they "provide better protection than clear jars or transparent dropper bottles." Retinol serums aren't quite as high-maintenance, but Dobos points out that "retinol is generally less stable than some newer retinoid technologies."

Close bottles tightly after each use, then stash them somewhere cool and dry. Like a linen closet or tucked inside a drawer, perhaps?

Pfefferman says "adapalene is more stable overall under all conditions." Differin contains 0.1% adapalene, and it's our top pick in our best retinol serums guide. Our tester raved about the "potent, effective, collagen-instigating, wrinkle-softening" gel.

"I could steer you toward a luxury retinol serum with all the bells and whistles, but for my money, this is the best retinoid on the (over-the-counter) market. And — bonus — it's not only effective but satisfyingly affordable," our tester glowed.

Our best-tested vitamin C serum also checks the packaging box: Drunk Elephant's C-Firma comes in an opaque outer container, one of the packaging types Dobos recommends.

Our tester raved that this serum is basically made of gold — and by that, she meant a 15% concentration of L-ascorbic acid. "The formula arrives in two parts — a liquid serum along with an accompanying vial of pristine vitamin C powder. You mix the two just before your first use, maximizing the stability of the vitamin C molecules and thus ensuring freshness," our tester wrote, adding that "the product remains potent for three to six months."

Most whitening gels, strips and trays contain either hydrogen peroxide or carbamide peroxide as the active ingredient. Hylan says proper storage is important for keeping at-home whitening products effective.

"Patients tell me that at-home whitening products didn't work at all for them," says Dr. Brad Hylan , a dentist based in Cleveland, Ohio. "In reality, they stored the product in a warm bathroom, causing it to go bad well before the expiration date and rendering it ineffective."

Remove whitening products from the hot, humid environment and stick them somewhere "cool, dark and dry." Hylan's recommendation? "A drawer in a bedroom or a linen closet separate from the bathroom, but check the box first since some will even tell you to store the product in the refrigerator."

Crest makes an at-home teeth whitening kit that uses hydrogen peroxide and has earned the American Dental Association (ADA) Seal of Acceptance.

"I usually recommend Crest Whitestrips because they use hydrogen peroxide, and it is tested, effective and [they've] been around longer than other companies," says Dr. Fatima Khan , a Houston-based dentist. Research shows that hydrogen peroxide is more effective at removing stains and whitening natural enamel than other whitening agents, including baking soda and sodium chlorite.

Taking jewelry off near a sink is risky business, but you know what's even worse? Storing your favorite pieces in a hot, humid bathroom in the first place. According to Nishit Mehta, founder and CEO of La Joya Jewelry , diamonds and solid gold jewelry can typically handle the heat and moisture, but pearls, sterling silver and plated jewelry "will suffer immediate, irreversible damage."

The reason? Mehta says the shower's steam "will literally eat away the pearl's luster," cause sterling silver to "tarnish at an accelerated rate" and "break down the base metals" beneath gold-plated jewelry.

And if you want to stay on the safe side, Mehta recommends keeping all of your jewels — especially your engagement ring — out of any room with constant temperature fluctuations since that causes metals to expand and contract. "Although this change is microscopic, over time, it can compromise the settings, causing you to lose a stone," he adds.

You guessed it: Jewelry is best kept in cool, dry and dark places, like a fabric-lined jewelry box that is kept away from direct sunlight and high humidity.

Once you've moved your jewelry out of the bathroom, a tiered box with separate compartments can help keep your most prized pieces organized and separated. Here, you can lay out your necklaces and bracelets in the two drawers, then store smaller pieces — earrings, rings and brooches — in the top layer with the clear window.

Sunscreen can be sensitive to heat. "Repeated exposure to heat and humidity can cause instability of the base formula and active ingredients over time just like any other cosmetic," Dobos says, noting that "sunscreen products undergo rigorous stability testing."

"Storing sunscreen in a cooler location helps preserve the product as intended," Dobos advises. Sure, this applies to your steamy bathroom, but it should also be top of mind when you're out and about. "Leaving it in really hot sun or in a hot car would be a really bad scenario," she warns, adding that "the interior temperature of a car can easily exceed 130°F within an hour when parked in the sun."

The American Academy of Dermatology Association says to ditch any spoiled sunscreen with an obvious change in color, a different or foul odor, signs of separation or a dry and flaky consistency.

Whichever sunscreen you use, proper storage matters. If you're looking for an affordable option to keep on hand, Neutrogena earned high marks in our testing for the best sunscreens — the dermatologist-backed favorite is water-resistant, fast-absorbing and has a non-greasy matte finish

You're already doing one thing right if you're wearing your retainer or mouth guard every night, but Dr. Karin Grinbaum, an orthodontist and owner of Smiles + Grins in New York City, says you should take things one step further. Yep, take your retainer or mouth guard out of the bathroom altogether. "If left in a humid environment, then moisture can encourage mold," she tells me.

Not to mention that, as Grinbaum points out, toilets disperse bacteria with every flush. "It's best to keep things that are meant to go in your mouth covered or in a case away from these aerosol droplets," she adds.

Make sure it dries completely, then place it in a well-ventilated case, Grinbaum says. Store it in your nightstand, in a linen closet or somewhere away from the steam. Another tip from Grinbaum: "Make sure to keep the case clean as well, not just the appliance."

This case checks the boxes Grinbaum recommends: Vent holes on both sides allow for airflow, and it's dishwasher-safe for easy cleaning between uses.

Is your signature scent smelling a bit off? Humidity probably isn't the main culprit here, but fluctuating temperatures can affect your fragrance over time. "Perfumes are carefully balanced mixtures of volatile aromatic compounds, and exposure to heat, sunlight, and oxygen can gradually alter the scent profile," Dobos says.

Always keep your fragrances in their original bottles and make sure they're tightly closed between spritzes. Stow them somewhere cool and dark — "a dresser drawer, closet shelf, or cabinet away from windows is generally ideal," suggests Dobos. And while some serious collectors swear by refrigerating their bottles, Dobos says it's unnecessary unless you plan on holding on to a rare or valuable fragrance for decades.

articles.title: Moment Peter Kay gatecrashes North West Tonight weather
articles.summary: The comedian interrupted North West Tonight weather presenter Molly Brewer as she gave her report.
articles.body:
Comedian Peter Kay gatecrashed a BBC weather report live on air.

BBC North West Tonight's Molly Brewer was presenting her report when Kay joined her on screen.

The Bolton comedian's impromptu appearance was reminiscent of when he famously interrupted the late Dianne Oxberry's forecast in 2011, and declared she "made it sunshine for everybody".

It came as Kay was speaking about staging a one-off show at Blackpool's Opera House next month to raise funds for vital heart treatment in the United States for 19-year-old Fin Cormack from Prenton, Merseyside.

Peter Kay reveals extra gig for teen's heart treatment

articles.title: Canal killer John Sweeney, who dismembered victims, dies in jail
articles.summary: John Sweeney was serving a whole-life sentence after being convicted in 2011 of the two murders.
articles.body:
A double killer who murdered and dismembered two women before dumping their bodies in canals in London and the Netherlands has died in prison.

John Sweeney, 69, was serving a whole-life sentence after being convicted in 2011 of the murders of his former girlfriends.

Paula Fields, 31, was killed in London. Parts of her body were found in six holdalls floating in Regent's Canal in Camden in February 2001. Her head, hands and feet were never recovered.

Melissa Halstead, 33, from the US, was killed in 1990. Her dismembered body was found in a canal in Rotterdam, but she was not identified for 18 years.

Sweeney is understood to have died at HMP Whitemoor in Cambridgeshire on 14 August.

Police found hundreds of violent paintings and poems at Sweeney's north London home, including artwork depicting a bloodied axe and references to himself as the "Scalp Hunter".

Police suspected he had murdered other former partners who had not been seen for years.

He had previously been jailed for attempting to murder former girlfriend Delia Balmer in a 1994 axe attack in north London.

Balmer later wrote a memoir about her experiences, which was adapted into the ITV drama Until I Kill You in 2024.

A prison service spokesperson described the crimes as "horrific" and said their thoughts remained with the victims and their loved ones.

As with all deaths in custody, the Prisons and Probation Ombudsman is investigating.

articles.title: Former Texas high school teacher arrested after probe into inappropriate student relationship
articles.summary: Holly Adams, an Angleton High School teacher, faces charges of tampering with evidence and furnishing alcohol to minors after a year-long investigation.
articles.body: A former Texas schoolteacher was arrested Tuesday amid allegations of inappropriate relationships with students, nearly one year after authorities began investigating her. Holly Adams, who taught at Angleton High School near Houston, is charged with one count of tampering with evidence and two counts of purchasing or furnishing alcohol to a minor, the Brazoria County Sheriff's Office said. The probe began after a student told school staff that Adams was having an inappropriate relationship with a former student, KTRK-TV reported. TEXAS SUBSTITUTE TEACHER ACCUSED OF IMPROPER RELATIONSHIP WITH STUDENT, ALARMING PARENTS The student told school officials that the victim FaceTime-called him over the summer from a bedroom in Adams' house and that the bed was covered in nude photos of her, according to the news outlet. Another image depicted Adams and the former student cuddling, the report states. Adams reportedly invited students to her home to perform chores, and she allegedly admitted to speaking with three members of the school baseball team on Snapchat. HIGH SCHOOL TEACHER WHO ALLEGEDLY HAD SEX WITH STUDENT IN CLOSET NOW FACES CHARGES INVOLVING MORE TEENS Many female teachers who sexually abuse male students sometimes convice themselves that the relationship is legitimate, said Gail Saltz, MD, Clinical Associate Professor of Psychiatry at Weill Cornell Medical College. "They're more likely to be psychologically both grooming their victim, but also what's called self grooming," Saltz told Fox News Digital. "They are convincing themselves that what they are doing is having an intimate, romantic relationship that is benefiting the victim as well." Saltz noted that the damage done to the male students is just as damaging as female victims. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It is easily as damaging in terms of, you've been abused by an adult. And that adult took advantage of your trust," she said. "That violated boundaries that you weren't ready for." Adams was taken to the Brazoria County Detention Center and released on a $26,000 bond the same day. She no longer works for the Angleton Independent School District, a spokesperson told Fox News Digital. Fox News Digital has reached out to the sheriff's office.

articles.title: Nvidia sales soar on rapid buildout of AI data centres
articles.summary: Chipmaker's $96bn quarter beat forecasts as demand for AI hardware continues to accelerate.
articles.body:
Chipmaker Nvidia has reported another huge jump in sales as the global push to build artificial intelligence (AI) systems continues at a rapid pace.

The company said on Wednesday it brought in $96bn (£71bn) in revenue during the second quarter, more than double from a year ago. And it expects revenue of $108bn next quarter.

"AI has reached its inflection point," CEO Jensen Huang said in prepared remarks, describing the infrastructure buildout as going "at full steam."

The revenue figures beat Wall Street's expectations, leading Nvidia shares to rise about 4% in after hours trading.

The company's data centre division alone generated $89bn last quarter, up 117% from a year ago, underscoring just how much of the industry now depends on Nvidia's hardware.

Essentially every notable tech company building AI tools and infrastructure, including Amazon, Meta, Google, Microsoft, use Nvidia chips to do so.

Financial analysts said the strong results highlight Nvidia's ongoing momentum.

Matt Britzman, senior equity analyst at Hargreaves Lansdown, called it "another monster set of results," noting that revenue and earnings both topped forecasts.

He said the guidance for next quarter "points to revenue comfortably above $110bn."

Nvidia's growing financial strength has also reshaped its role in the sector.

It has become a backer to those that rely on its chips, providing some funding to the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX to help continue the costly buildout of AI infrastructure.

Its financial success and processors are now central the AI boom, powering the data centres used to train and run AI models.

Demand for that computing muscle has helped transform Nvidia into the world's most valuable firm, with a market capitalisation above $5tn.

Competition is emerging – from customers designing their own processors and from cheaper suppliers in China – but the latest numbers suggest those challenges remain limited for now.

With around 40% of the US stock market concentrated in ten companies heavily invested in AI, Nvidia's fortunes matter far beyond Silicon Valley.

articles.title: Hetland Hall Hotel expansion plans could deliver 60 jobs
articles.summary: The operators of the Hetland Hall Hotel near Dumfries want to add bedrooms, an events space and lodges.
articles.body:
Plans to expand a country house hotel in the south of Scotland could deliver up to 60 jobs to the area.

The RAD Hotel Group has lodged an application to extend its Hetland Hall Hotel at Carrutherstown in Dumfries and Galloway.

It would include 26 extra bedrooms, a spa and wellness facility and the creation of a new wedding and events space along with 10 woodland lodges.

A planning statement submitted in support of the plans said they would "create a unique visitor experience that embraces the exceptional landscape setting of Hetland Hall".

Hetland House was originally built in 1868 and has been expanded over the years and was used, for a time, as a seminary.

It became a hotel in 1985 and has operated as such since then.

If approved, the plans would see a two-storey extension added along with the woodland lodges.

The company said its plans had aimed to provide additional floorspace while respecting the architectural and historical significance of the building.

"Hetland Hall is an established country house hotel and recognised visitor destination within Dumfries and Galloway," said the statement supporting the plans.

It said the proposals represented a "significant investment in the continued evolution of the hotel" which aimed to "broaden the hotel's tourism offer".

The company said it could also deliver economic benefits by increasing visitor capacity, improving its wedding offering and creating new jobs.

It added it could also see increased visitor spending in the wider area, support local suppliers and strengthen the region's tourism sector.

The group said the proposals could secure the long-term future of the building through "sensitive expansion".

It will be up to Dumfries and Galloway Council's planning committee to decide - at a later date - whether the plans should go ahead.

Hetland Hall is one of a number of hotels operated by the RAD Group across Scotland.

The group was founded in 1999 with the purchase of Lochside House Hotel near New Cumnock, but it now owns a "portfolio of 10 stunning venues".

Among its other sites are Seamill Hydro, Fairfield House Hotel, Dalmeny Park and Lochgreen House.

Building once known as 'first hotel in Scotland' to become business hub

articles.title: Body camera video from deadly Jacksonville officer-involved shooting of Asia Bennett released
articles.summary: The Jacksonville Sheriff's Office has released body camera video showing the events leading up to the deadly officer-involved shooting of 22-year-old Asia Be...
articles.body:
The Jacksonville Sheriff's Office has released body camera video showing the events leading up to the deadly officer-involved shooting of 22-year-old Asia Bennett on August 11.

Bennett's family previously held a press conference along with civil rights attorney Ben Crump calling for a quick release of the footage to the public.

According to JSO, officers responded to a home on Westdale Drive around 10:45 p.m. after receiving a domestic violence-related call from a person who was in a relationship with Bennett.

The video shows officers arriving at the home and speaking with a man who told them his girlfriend was inside the residence with a knife. Moments later, Bennett exits the house carrying several items. Officers repeatedly ordered her to drop the objects, and Bennett complied for everything except the knife, which she continued to hold.

Throughout the encounter, Bennett can be heard repeatedly yelling that he "beat" her as officers continued giving commands for her to drop the weapon. Bennett refused, and repeatedly told officers to kill her.

When Bennett did not comply with commands and moved toward officers, according to JSO, that's when Officer Gaitten fired her weapon. After Bennett fell to the ground, officers continued ordering her to drop the knife. A second shot was then fired.

First Coast News Crime and Safety Analyst Ken Jefferson reviewed the body camera footage and said the situation escalated because Bennett did not comply with officers' commands to drop the knife.

"When she's not obeying the commands to drop the knife, the officers use deadly force to stop the threat," Jefferson said. "Now there are those that'll say, well, she only had a knife and you had a gun. Why didn't you just try to talk to her or whatever? If she's advancing on you with a knife, statistics have shown that a person with a knife can get up on you much quicker than you can draw your gun. Even though their guns were already drawn, you don't wanna wait until the person has the opportunity to use that knife against you."

However, Jefferson questions whether the second shot was necessary after Bennett was on the ground.

"My personal opinion on that, if she's on the ground and they're yards away from her, talk the knife out of her hand until she surrenders it as opposed to taking a second shot because they were far enough away where they, in my opinion, that she couldn't do any harm to them," Jefferson said.

"I just don't see where it's necessary for the second shot. I can understand the first shot when she's advancing with the knife towards him, but when she is shot and goes down, she's now disabled. She's, she's injured and she can't get up," Jefferson said.

Jefferson also said domestic violence calls are among the most dangerous situations officers respond to, but believes officers may have overly delayed approaching Bennett after the shooting.

"They waited a couple of minutes before they did advance to take the knife out of her hand and handcuffed her and got EMS there. I believe that that could have been done sooner so that she can get the necessary aid that she needed from the medical staff," Jefferson said.

Bennett's family has retained civil rights attorney Ben Crump to represent them. Crump is set to hold a press conference Thursday, Aug. 27 at noon in Jacksonville.

JSO said the State Attorney's Office is conducting an independent investigation into the shooting, as is normal for shootings involving law enforcement.

articles.title: A man searching a Polish scrapyard for car parts found an 1,800-year-old Roman-era shield containing cremated human bones
articles.summary: Rest of World News: An old iron fitting found among scrap metal in eastern Poland has turned out to be part of a burial that disappeared from the archaeological record lo.
articles.body: An old iron fitting found among scrap metal in eastern Poland has turned out to be part of a burial that disappeared from the archaeological record long ago. The object, recovered in Hrubieszów, is a shield boss dating to around the 2nd century CE. More unexpectedly, traces of cremated human bone were still preserved within soil lodged inside it.The discovery does not amount to a complete grave. The shield is gone, as are the other objects that would normally help archaeologists understand who was buried and when. Yet the surviving piece carries several clues about a cremation ceremony associated with the Przeworsk culture and communities linked with the Vandals.What looked like scrap turned out to be an ancient shield bossAccording to Archaeology News Online Magazine, the object was noticed by Włodzimierz Starykiewicz while he was searching a scrapyard for old motorcycle and car parts. Covered in corrosion, it did not immediately resemble something that had spent centuries underground. Starykiewicz nevertheless suspected that the unusual iron fitting might have an archaeological value and contacted the Stanisław Staszic Museum in Hrubieszów.Museum specialists identified it as an umbo, the reinforced fitting that sat at the centre of an ancient shield. Its pointed form is characteristic of a type used during the Roman period. The piece dates to the 2nd century CE.An umbo had a practical job. Fixed over the centre of the shield, it strengthened a vulnerable part of the wooden structure and helped protect the hand of the person carrying it. The wooden shield itself has long since disappeared.Soil trapped inside the shield boss revealed traces of a cremationThere was still a small quantity of hardened soil inside the iron fitting when it was recovered. Rather than clearing it out, Starykiewicz left the material in place. The soil contained fragments of burnt human bone. Examination also found evidence that the iron had been subjected to intense heat, consistent with its presence on a funeral pyre. The combination gives archaeologists a reason to believe the shield was part of a cremation burial rather than simply an abandoned or discarded piece of military equipment.Some traces in the soil also point towards the object's later history. Crop stubble was present, suggesting that the fitting had lain in cultivated ground before eventually being recovered and taken to the scrapyard. It is a small amount of surviving material, but it connects the object to a much larger event: the burning and burial of a person more than 1,800 years ago.The shield boss points to a Przeworsk culture cremation burialThe find belongs to the archaeological world of the Przeworsk culture, an Iron Age and Roman-period society whose communities occupied substantial areas of what is now Poland. Around Hrubieszów, archaeologists associate some burials with groups connected to the Vandals.Cremation was an established funerary practice among communities in the region. Personal belongings and equipment could be placed with the deceased before or during the funeral, meaning that weapons and other fittings sometimes survived even when the human remains were heavily altered by fire.The shield boss may therefore have belonged to someone buried with equipment associated with warfare. That does not establish that the individual was a warrior, however, and the surviving remains cannot determine whether the person was male or female.The missing parts of the grave make the question harder to answer.Farming and time erased much of the original burialA burial containing a shield boss might once have included considerably more. Swords, spearheads, javelin points, belt fittings and brooches are among the objects that can occur in comparable graves.None of them accompanied the umbo. The shield itself would have offered little chance of survival. Ancient shields were largely constructed from wood, with leather or other organic coverings sometimes added. Unlike the iron fitting, those materials generally disappear after centuries in the ground.Agriculture may have contributed to the loss of the burial's original arrangement. The object appears to have been lying in a cultivated area, and later disturbance seems to have separated it from whatever remained of the grave. By the time it reached the scrapyard, its archaeological context had effectively vanished.The shield also hints at contact with RomeThe form of the umbo sits within a wider pattern of interaction between communities north of the Roman frontier and the Roman world. Przeworsk material culture contains objects and styles that show connections with Roman military equipment.Such similarities do not necessarily mean that the equipment was directly imported from the Roman army. Goods, ideas and manufacturing techniques could travel in several ways, including trade, warfare and contact between neighbouring communities.The shield fitting is therefore useful beyond the question of the individual burial. It belongs to a period when communities outside the Roman Empire were not isolated from what was happening across the frontier.Still, without the rest of the grave, there is only so much the object can reveal.Museum hopes the original finder will come forwardThe museum is now trying to establish where the shield boss was originally recovered. Staff have appealed to the person who brought it to the scrapyard, hoping that even an approximate location might be remembered.A rough findspot could make a significant difference. Archaeologists might be able to inspect the surrounding area, look for additional material or determine whether the shield boss came from a larger archaeological site.For now, the iron fitting remains an isolated survivor of a burial that has otherwise disappeared. The cremated bone inside it is a rare connection to the person who was once placed beside the shield.What began as an inconspicuous piece of corroded metal among discarded vehicle parts has provided a small, but tangible, record of a funerary practice in eastern Poland nearly two millennia ago.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: For centuries, flood-hit corridor was key route of Himalayan trade
articles.summary: South Asia News: The Himalayan corridor, particularly Rasuwagadhi, devastated by the flash flood had served for more than 260 years as one of Nepal’s key trans-Himalay.
articles.body: The Himalayan corridor, particularly Rasuwagadhi, devastated by the flash flood had served for more than 260 years as one of Nepal’s key trans-Himalayan arteries, carrying traders, pilgrims and armies before becoming a major gateway for Chinese electronics, garments, footwear and electric vehicles entering the country.Long before trucks climbed Bhote Koshi valley, mule caravans carried rice and other grain from Nepal north to Gyirong, where traders exchanged them for Tibetan salt and wool. Salt, highly valued in Nepal’s middle hills, travelled farther south towards India. Newar merchant communities also settled in Tibetan trading towns.The corridor had great strategic importance. Gorkha (Nepal district from which the community derives its name) captured Nuwakot in 1744 partly to control the lucrative Tibet trade. Nepalese troops later used the route during invasions of Tibet in 1788 and 1791 before Chinese and Tibetan forces counter-attacked in 1792. Jung Bahadur Rana built the Rasuwagadhi fort at the frontier while preparing another invasion in 1855. The 171-year-old fort still stood beside the modern Rasuwagadhi-Gyirong customs crossing.Political changes after 1950 and new motor roads gradually ended the caravan economy, but trade through the mountain gap only changed form. Rasuwagadhi had in later years become an unlikely gateway for Nepal’s EV boom. More than 6,500 Chinese electric cars, jeeps, vans and minibuses entered through the crossing in 2025-26, Rasuwa Customs figures showed. Vehicles awaiting clearance regularly packed the customs area, turning the narrow Himalayan settlement into a temporary automobile depot.That concentration of vehicles and cargo had also become a disaster risk. The July 2025 flood swept away numerous newly imported EVs and cargo vehicles. In the latest deluge, hundreds of 40-foot shipping containers parked along Timure riverbanks were dislodged and swept downstream, acting like floating battering rams as they struck bridge pillars, road embankments and power transmission towers.The flood also destroyed Miteri Sanghu, or Friendship Bridge, across Lhende/Koshi river. Rebuilt after 2015 earthquake and repaired after the 2025 flood, the bridge lost its supporting abutments within seconds, severing the physical Nepal-China border link — the same passage through which salt and wool once came down and rice went up.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: FDA approves breakthrough drug daraxonrasib to treat pancreatic cancer
articles.summary: Experts have hailed the drug, daraxonrasib, as a game changer for one of the world's deadliest cancers.
articles.body:
The US Food and Drug Administration has approved a treatment for pancreatic cancer that, in clinical trials, nearly doubled the overall survival time for patients.

The drug, daraxonrasib, sold under the brand name Rasonque and manufactured by Revolution Medicines, appears to be a breakthrough in treating one of the world's deadliest cancers.

A late-stage clinical trial with 500 patients found those who took the daily pill had an average survival time of 13.2 months, compared to 6.6 months for those on chemotherapy.

The FDA said the drug provided a "critical new option for patients facing an extraordinarily difficult and historically hard-to-treat cancer".

Daraxonrasib helps prevent the spread of cancer by locking onto and shutting off the mutated KRAS gene, which is in more than 90% of pancreatic tumours and spurs cancer growth.

Each year, roughly 67,000 people in the US are diagnosed with pancreatic cancer, which has the highest mortality rate of all major cancers, according to the American Cancer Society..

Pancreatic cancer is often spotted late and is notoriously difficult to treat. More than half of those with pancreatic cancer die within three months of diagnosis.

In 2025, the FDA granted the drug a "Breakthrough Therapy" designation, given to treatments for serious conditions that warrant an expedited review.

The agency then approved the drug six months ahead of the regulatory deadline because it "showed unprecedented results in an area of high unmet need", said Angelo de Claro, director of the the agency's Oncology Center of Excellence.

The most common side effects of the treatment were rash, diarrhoea, nausea, fatigue and vomiting, the FDA said. About 44% of patients on daraxonrasib experienced severe side effects, compared to 57.5% treated with chemotherapy in the trial.

Former US Senator Ben Sasse, who announced in December he had been diagnosed with Stage 4 pancreatic cancer, is in a clinical trial for the drug and has said it has helped shrink his tumours.

articles.title: Girl Scouts denies teaching religion amid scrutiny of Muslim faith awards, mosque visits
articles.summary: The Girls Scouts of the USA says independent faith groups run optional Islamic programs after reports alleged mosque-based troops taught prayer and hijab lessons.
articles.body: Girls Scouts of the USA pushed back Wednesday on reports that mosque-based troops incorporated Islamic prayer, hijab lessons and faith-specific patches into scouting activities across several states, saying outside faith organizations independently run the optional programs. "Girl Scouts is proudly for every girl. Contrary to misinformation circulating online, Girl Scouts is not a religious organization and does not teach religion. For more than a century, we've welcomed girls of every faith and background," a GSUSA spokesperson said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "Our national My Promise, My Faith pin invites girls to connect the Girl Scout Law with their own faith. Any other faith-based patches are developed by independent faith organizations, not GSUSA, and participation in these programs is always optional." EL-SAYED'S DEFENSE OF SHARIA LAW STANCE SPARKS ONLINE ERUPTION FROM CHRISTIANS, CONSERVATIVES: 'HE'S DONE' GSUSA’s own materials state that the organization has approved religious-recognition programs created by faith groups and permits their insignia on official uniforms. A chart currently hosted on its national website says each religious organization develops and administers its own curriculum. The chart lists four Islamic recognitions — Bismillah, In the Name of Allah, Quratula’in and Muslimeen — alongside programs for Christian, Jewish, Buddhist, Hindu, Baha’i and other faith communities. It directs Muslim families to the Islamic Committee on Girl Scouting. A 2025 Girl Scouts of Orange County, California, faith toolkit says the Islamic Committee on Girl Scouting provides Muslim Girl Scouts with activity booklets and medals. The toolkit also lists churches, mosques and temples as possible venues for faith events. A separate All About Islam Patch website aimed at Girls Scouts requires every age level to complete sections on all Five Pillars of Islam and at least three activities. Options include attempting a partial fast, donating to charity and completing a Five Pillars worksheet. The program is hosted separately from GSUSA's national website. TEXAS TEEN TELLS CONGRESS HE RECEIVED DEATH THREATS AFTER REVEALING ISLAMIC BOOTH AT HIGH SCHOOL Moms for Liberty New Jersey Ambassador Alexandra Bougher criticized the religious recognition programs in a statement to Fox News Digital Wednesday, arguing that faith-specific badges could exclude girls who do not share the beliefs required to earn them. "No Girl Scout chapter should push one faith over another by incentivizing it with badges some girls, because of their own faith, will not be able to earn," Bougher said. "Girl Scouts should rededicate itself to its true mission instead of getting involved in ideological battles that exist to endorse a particular faith or exclude young scouts of another faith from earning merit badges." The scrutiny followed a report Saturday by White House correspondent Natalie Winters alleging that mosque-based troops had incorporated Quran study, Islamic prayer, Ramadan observances and hijab activities into Girl Scout programming. The report cited programs in California, Illinois, New York and Virginia. The cited examples involved local troops, councils and faith organizations rather than a compulsory national curriculum. GSUSA’s website has also highlighted Orange County Muslim troops that organized an Open Mosque Day for Girl Scout families. ONE OF NATION'S LARGEST CHRISTIAN FOSTER AGENCIES WILL NOT ALLOW LGBTQ COUPLES TO ADOPT CHILDREN American Heritage Girls (AHG), a Christian scouting organization founded in 1995 as an alternative to Girl Scouts, emphasized its upfront disclosure of religious programming in a statement to Fox News Digital. "American Heritage Girls is unapologetically Christ-centered, and we lead with that identity rather than obscure it. Every family is told upfront, before they ever join a troop, that our programming — including our curriculum, activities, or any other facet of the ministry — is built around a relationship with Jesus," an AHG spokesperson said. The spokesperson said AHG discloses what girls will learn from the outset and vets outside materials for consistency with its Christian mission. "We welcome girls from all faith backgrounds, but we don't soften or hide our core beliefs and values," the spokesperson continued. And parents appreciate that."

articles.title: Over 61,000 wait for kidney transplants
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: India faces a widening gap between demand for kidney transplants and the availability of donor organs, with 61,668 patients on the waiting .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India faces a widening gap between demand for kidney transplants and the availability of donor organs, with 61,668 patients on the waiting list, nearly five times the number of kidney transplants performed as of Feb 9, a parliamentary standing committee has said.The committee on health and family welfare has recommended that kidney transplant facilities be expanded to at least three govt medical colleges in large states and one in every small state and UT, besides setting time-bound targets to increase organ retrieval centres and transplant infrastructure, particularly in underserved and hilly regions.India performed 11,558 living-donor and 1,918 deceased-donor kidney transplants in 2024, while 61,668 patients remained on the waiting list as of Feb 9. The committee — in its report tabled in the recently concluded monsoon session of Parliament — said the figures highlight the widening mismatch between demand and capacity and the continued dependence on living donors.It said transplant activity remains concentrated in a handful of states and metropolitan centres, including Delhi, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Gujarat and Karnataka, leaving access uneven across the country.The committee attributed the shortage partly to India’s low deceased-organ donation rates, citing social misconceptions, inadequate awareness, limited organ retrieval infrastructure and procedural bottlenecks. It has called for a nationwide behavioural-change campaign and stronger hospital-based organ retrieval and transplant coordination systems.Data from the National Organ and Tissue Transplant Organisation for 2019-23 showed that women constituted 63.8% of living organ donors, while men accounted for 69.8% of transplant recipients. The committee has sought a study to determine whether socioeconomic, cultural, financial or gender-related barriers contribute to the disparity.Get the latest India News and Live updates. SEOUL, Aug 26 (Reuters) - Nine South Koreans working on a hydropower ‌plant are missing, and 10 ‌others stranded, following a massive flash flood along ​the Nepal-Tibet border, South Korea's Foreign Ministry said late on Wednesday.

The workers were employed by Korea Energy and ‌Doosan Enerbility ⁠Co, the ministry said, adding that Nepal has deployed a ⁠rescue team to search the affected area.

South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun ​held an ​emergency meeting ​with government officials ‌and said a team of police, emergency services and foreign ministry officials will fly to Kathmandu on Thursday, the ministry said.

Cho plans to hold ‌a phone call with ​his Nepalese counterpart on ​Thursday, it ​said.

Another 10 South Korean ‌workers affiliated with Doosan ​Enerbility were ​stranded in the area and awaiting a helicopter sent by Nepalese ​authorities to ‌evacuate them.

articles.title: Rahul Gandhi questions India PM Narendra Modi's 'culture shock' comment over women swearing at CJP protest
articles.summary: Rahul Gandhi's comments renew the debate over gender disparity in reactions to insults hurled at PM Narendra Modi.
articles.body:
Recent footage of young women swearing during a protest in India has sparked an unusual debate: are expletives worse when they come from women?

The latest to weigh in has been opposition MP Rahul Gandhi who criticised Prime Minister Narendra Modi's description of seeing young women swearing as a "culture shock".

"If boys swear, there is no problem and it is allowed. But if a girl swears, it is a cultural shock," Gandhi said.

The protesters had been directing their anger at the government and some of the foul language targeted the prime minister, leading to outrage among his supporters, with even many critics of Modi's politics saying the women had crossed a line.

The protests ended a month ago, but Rahul Gandhi's remarks have renewed the debate over how female activism, women voicing their views, stridently - even with expletives - are viewed in the country.

It started last month when some young women used foul language against the prime minister during the weeks-long Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protests in Delhi and other cities, seeking education reforms.

Modi himself addressed the issue in a selfie video where he said it was "a culture shock" to see young women using expletives, but added that he forgave them.

The prime minister, however, did not comment on the violent police crackdown against the protesters or support women who said they had been trolled and had received rape threats for attending the CJP protests.

At the weekend, Rahul Gandhi, who serves as the leader of the opposition in the lower house of the Indian parliament, criticised Modi's "culture shock" comment at a gathering of students in the western city of Pune.

Pointing out that both male and female protesters had used foul language during the protest over exam paper leaks, he asked why was Modi only talking about women?

His comments came weeks after posters and videos of female protesters insulting Modi went viral on social media.

As police opened an investigation into abusive posts, a 15-year-old girl became caught up in the centre of the controversy, with trolls sending her abuses and threats on social media.

The teenager put out a video apologising for her language and seeking forgiveness. She also said that she had taken down her video, but the outrage continued.

Her mother, a single parent, told the local press that the controversy had forced them to move home a number of times.

Modi had been more conciliatory in his vertical video shared on Instagram after the protest had ended. "Some naughty children used extremely abusive expletives which have no place in a civilised society," he said. "They abused me, they also abused my late mother. It was deeply disturbing."

Addressing the outrage from his supporters, he said he understood their anger. "It's a culture shock. How can our daughters use such language? But I want to say that mistakes are made in childhood and it's an opportunity to fix them."

At the Pune event, Gandhi said Modi's singling out the gender of protesters was rooted in patriarchy.

"What is the mindset that a girl has a place while boys get full freedom? They can do whatever they want, if they want to swear, they can swear... We have to smash this patriarchy," he said.

Journalist Namita Bhandare who writes a popular column on gender issues in the Hindustan Times newspaper told the BBC that contrary to what people say, many "women in India of course swear, it's not new".

In many villages of northern Indian, an important wedding ritual involves women from bride's family singing a medley of expletives while welcoming the groom's party - a tradition that nobody finds offensive.

So, Bhandare says, describing what was said at Jantar Mantar as culture shock and calling women out for using swear words shows "double standards" because politicians of all hues, including the prime minister, have used slurs against women when it suited them.

In his Independence Day speech in 2022, Modi called on Indians to fight misogyny . His government runs a number of scheme aimed at uplifting women and Modi enjoys tremendous popularity among female voters.

But on many instances, Modi and his party colleagues have been criticised for being disrespectful to women. A number of senior party leaders have been called out for misogynistic comments about women's clothing. Modi himself has invited criticism for using terms such as "Jersey cow" in a 2004 rally and "50 crore ki girlfriend" ["girlfriend worth 500m rupee"] in another event in 2012.

Such criticism is not confined to the BJP. Many opposition politicians, including those from Gandhi's Congress party, have also faced similar allegations. A Congress leader in Kerala state recently sparked outrage with remarks about using women to make false complaints against political opponents.

"Women are treated so shabbily and it's so easy to target them. And then when they use profanity, then everyone asks, how can our girls cuss and swear," says Bhandare.

Social activist Sunil Jalan, who's been running a Gali Bandh Abhiyan (a campaign aimed at stopping use of cuss words) since 2014, says "we must focus on swearing, not on the gender of who uses them".

In a survey by his NGO last year, 55% of the more than 70,000 participants from across 28 Indian states and eight federally-administered territories admitted to using foul language.

The question asked was straightforward: how often do you hear or use expletives that target mothers, sisters or daughters?

Their 2025 Gali [expletive] Map of India showed very high prevalence rates in the north - 80% in Delhi, 78% in Punjab and 74% in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar states. Most southern states were below 44% and it was between 15% and 18% in the north-east.

Jalan says this is the first time in the country that a dialogue over foul language is taking place, "and hopefully something good will come out of it".

"It's a very serious issue. It's a virus that's spread through society. Comedy, jokes and films have normalised swearing and it needs to be reined in," he says.

But many of India's Gen Z do not see profanity in the same way.

"Profanity and protest have gone hand in hand for ages. There's a shock-and-awe factor to it, which is fundamental to protest," CJP spokesperson Sourav Das told the BBC earlier. "It may be distasteful to some people and not to others. But it absolutely can't be criminal."

And such language is hardly confined to street protests. Profanity and personal attacks have increasingly become part of India's public discourse, from television debates to courtrooms and even parliament.

A video that went viral earlier this week showed a female presenter on Indian government-owned Doordarshan channel trying to control a temple priest who let out a volley of cuss words at a Congress party spokesman who then retaliated in the same language.

In 2023, BJP MP Ramesh Bidhuri was extensively criticised for using Islamophobic slurs against a Muslim MP and threatening him in Parliament. As outrage grew, he later said he regretted his statement.

Sociologist Shiv Vishwanathan says "the use of expletives is the symptom of a deeper breakdown of democracy, it shows there's end of discussion and a lack of respect".

When expletives are used inside Parliament and courts, he says, "it shows there's a breakdown of language, there's a decline of argument and decline of democracy".

The use of profanity by protesters is because "when there's a weaker sense of respect, expletives become a response".

articles.title: Treatment involving patient's family cuts mental health hospital admissions, study finds
articles.summary: The approach focuses on the patient priorities, seeing the same clinicians, and involving people close to them.
articles.body:
Involving a patient's family and friends as part of a new approach to mental health treatment makes it three times less likely they will be admitted to psychiatric hospital, research has found.

Patients rated their recovery and quality of life more highly than those who were treated in the traditional way, it also found.

It is the first major study of Open Dialogue, a way of providing treatment and organising mental health services that involves focusing on the patient's priorities, seeing the same clinicians, and involving people close to them.

But, the trial, in five NHS trust areas, found it did not stop patients suffering relapses, and some critics say there needs to be further research into its effectiveness.

Dr Nihad Fathi has benefited from the approach after he felt his life started to spiral out of control as the Covid pandemic took hold in 2020.

By the next summer, problems in his work had left him feeling anxious, depressed and worthless. He felt like he was letting his clients down.

"It was so much pressure, stress," he said.

"I caught myself like a lost child and I didn't know what's going on in my mind," he said.

It was a terrifying time for his wife Farah. "At that stage, I didn't know what to do," she said.

For one of his sessions Nihad and Farah sit in a circle in their east London home with two clinicians – consultant psychiatrist Dr Bill Travers and community psychiatric nurse David Adebayo.

They have been working with Nihad for five years and the NHS trust they work for, North East London NHS Foundation Trust, has been using Open Dialogue with some of its community patients since 2019.

Open Dialogue was first devised in the 1980s in Finland. It is now used in more than 20 countries around the world, although the research into its effectiveness has been limited.

The idea is for a patient to regularly take part in "network meetings". As well as two Open Dialogue practitioners, these meetings also involve the friends, families, neighbours or colleagues of the patient. They then remain involved in the patient's recovery.

The sessions allow a free-flowing conversation about how the patient feels, what help they would like and how that may be achieved. It also allows the "network" to talk about what they have observed about the patient and their own feelings.

Dr Travers said although the network meetings were longer than a normal appointment, the patients need fewer of them.

"It enables you to reach a much firmer and deeper understanding of the underlying reasons for the problems and indeed to seek solutions that come very much from the person and their family," he said.

The study, led by University College London, involved 500 patients that had approached mental health services in crisis. They were split into two groups - one was entered into Open Dialogue, the other received treatment as usual.

Researchers found there was no significant difference in whether a patient had a relapse of their illness. But, as well as the reduction in need for psychiatric hospital, if patients in the Open Dialogue group did need to be admitted, the length of time they spent there was on average half that of the other group.

There were also improvements in how the patients felt about their wellbeing and recovery.

Dr Russell Razzaque, a consultant psychiatrist and the clinical lead on the trial, said this could have significant implications for how the NHS runs psychiatric care.

"There's a substantial reduction in cost because you're not spending all the money on inpatient beds, which are the most expensive part of the system," he said.

"So yes, you might be spending a bit more time in the community, but that is what the NHS wants."

However, consultant psychiatrist Dr Sameer Jauhar feels the benefits seen in the trial might be explained by the extra resources put into it, and that more research is needed.

"The important question is whether the distinctive, resource-intensive elements of Open Dialogue itself add benefit beyond good, adequately staffed community care. On the evidence of this trial, that question remains unresolved," he said.

But for Farah, Open Dialogue was the right intervention for Nihad.

"It needs somebody to hear him, somebody to understand him, how he feels, what he's trying to even to achieve. They are helping him and then he sees a better picture," she said.

If you are suffering distress or despair, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line

articles.title: Experts' five tips to make a rented property feel like home
articles.summary: Experts share tips on how to make a flat or house feel like your own without annoying the landlord.
articles.body:
It can be a balancing act making a rented property feel like your own.

You want somewhere that feels warm and personal but without spending a fortune changing a flat or house owned by someone else and making alterations that put a deposit at risk.

The good news is that transforming a rental doesn't have to mean a major renovation.

With a free weekend, a relatively small budget and a few clever changes, even a bland or tired-looking place can be spruced-up.

We asked B&Q chief executive Graham Bell and interior designers Lara Clarke and Lydia Lloyd for their top tips that won't break the bank or annoy a landlord.

Before making anything permanent, check what your tenancy agreement allows.

Bell, of DIY chain B&Q, says many landlords may be open to sensible improvements, particularly where something is being upgraded rather than fundamentally changed.

But getting permission first avoids an expensive argument when you move out.

Bell also says it is important to take time to prepare properly.

"The biggest mistake is that people don't plan enough," he says. "It's all the planning that goes into it that's important, making sure you have everything.

"My dad would tell me to always measure twice and cut once."

He recommends deciding exactly what you want to achieve, measuring the space and buying everything you need before you start.

Online tutorials can also help with relatively simple DIY projects.

If you don't want to spend money improving someone else's property, focus on temporary changes that can come with you when you move.

Bell recommends renter-friendly products such as stick-on tiles for the kitchen, suction storage products in the bathroom and expandable blinds that can be fitted without drilling.

Interior designer Clarke says artwork is probably the easiest way to make a rental feel more homely because it "instantly makes a space feel more occupied and finished".

She suggests looking for affordable vintage oil paintings, exhibition posters or framed sketches at antique markets, then securing them with command strips so they can be removed without leaving holes in the plaster.

Lighting is one of the quickest ways to transform a space.

Bell says rentals often come with "bright, bright lights", but swapping them out for something warmer can dramatically change the atmosphere of a room.

He suggests experimenting using lightbulbs or strip lighting with different tones. Strip lighting is often found in kitchens but a softer glow can change the whole feel of the space without requiring a major renovation.

Rather than depending on a single overhead light, Clarke recommends building up different sources from around the room.

"Mood lighting really helps make a space feel more cosy and homely," she says.

"Add table and floor lamps too and there are plenty of battery-powered options around now so you don't have to worry about finding a plug socket."

Clarke says the effect can be made even cosier by pairing lighting with soft furnishings, such as floor-to-ceiling curtains and scatter cushions in different colours and patterns.

A simple way to make a rented house stop feeling temporary is to create a corner that reflects who you are.

Lloyd, a home designer at M&S, says it doesn't need to cost a lot since a "few carefully chosen accessories [can] make a big difference".

She says: "Books, framed photographs, decorative objects and houseplants help tell your story and can make even a temporary space feel more personal and lived in."

To add a little something extra, Clarke suggests "sourcing characterful pieces".

"Avoid flatpack furniture," she says. "And source things from online marketplaces or antique markets for unique pieces that tell a story and make a space feel more lived-in and curated over time."

Lloyd believes scent is a "simple but powerful way to make a home feel inviting".

Buying candles, diffusers and room sprays "can help create a warm, cosy atmosphere, especially as we move into the colder months".

She recommends fragrances such as sandalwood, cedarwood, cinnamon and cardamom as they "are perfect for bringing a sense of comfort into the home".

She also suggests "adding layers of texture through cushions, throws and blankets" thinking about mixing materials like velvet, boucle or chunky knits.

articles.title: Iceland holds knife-edge referendum on EU - and it could be decided on fish
articles.summary: On Saturday, Iceland will vote on EU membership talks, amid economic and geopolitical tensions.
articles.body:
Inside a waterfront factory, workers in hairnets and blue overalls are sorting freshly caught cod and haddock, and machines process the fish into fillets, mostly bound for Europe.

Visir fishing boss Pétur Pálsson, who fears joining the European Union would cost Iceland jobs and drive factories abroad, says: "If we are in the EU, they will be the ones who make the policy."

On Saturday, voters in this island nation of almost 400,000 people will decide whether their country should resume talks on joining the EU. It is a referendum that polls suggest is too close to call.

Supporters think closer European ties could help tame Iceland's volatile currency and soaring cost of living.

Opponents say Iceland's sovereignty and control over "priceless" fishing waters are at stake, and would rather continue going it alone.

It is a fault line that has divided Icelanders for decades, but after winning a snap election in 2024 Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir's centre-left government pledged to hold a referendum by 2027.

Russia's war in Ukraine, sharpening Arctic rivalries and US President Donald Trump's tariff threats and designs on Greenland have accelerated that timetable.

"Things have been moving very rapidly with respect to geopolitical challenges," Finance Minister Daði Már Kristófersson tells the BBC, pushing Iceland's place in the world "up the agenda".

Iceland lies high in the North Atlantic, adjacent to a strategic stretch of sea called the GIUK gap, where Russian maritime activity is closely watched by the West.

It is a founding member of Nato, and yet has no military of its own.

One poll this week put the Yes vote ahead by 51.3% to 48.7%; an earlier poll had the two camps neck and neck.

"It's impossibly [hard] to predict," says Eirikur Bergmann, professor of politics at Bifröst University. "Both camps are throwing everything they have at it."

Kristoffersen's Liberal Reform party is a leading voice behind the Yes campaign.

He argues that EU membership would strengthen Iceland's security and trade position, and shield it from much bigger powers.

There's the economic case too. "We see the opportunity of joining the EU and adopting the euro as a very significant benefit to Icelandic companies and to the Icelandic general public," he says.

A Yes vote would kickstart negotiations with Brussels, but a second referendum would have to greenlight any final membership deal. The EU's 27 members would have to agree to it too.

A No vote would shelve talks for the time being.

Some Icelanders are expected to vote Yes as this is not the final referendum anyway. "We have to know what's in the package from the EU," says Reykjavik resident Anna Ragnarsdottir. "If we say no, we won't ever know."

Although outside the EU, Iceland is part of the European Economic Area (EEA) along with Norway and Liechtenstein, so it is part of the single market and the Schengen border-free zone.

Reykjavik opened EU accession talks two years after the devastating 2008 global financial crisis, but abandoned them in 2013.

Fishing was the biggest obstacle then, and remains a dealbreaker today.

Fish and marine industries account for almost 40% of Iceland's exports and many No voters are worried that under the EU's common fisheries policy they could cede some control of their lucrative fishing grounds.

Opposition leader Guðrún Hafsteinsdóttir, who leads the No campaign, vows Iceland's waters will never be shared.

Fishing is inseparable from Iceland's culture and political identity, and no politician ever could make that concession, says Prof Bergmann. "They'd be expelled from the country."

Iceland's government intends to carve out a "special arrangement" to protect fishing and agriculture, and the finance minister says they are confident of getting "some exemptions".

Non-EU member Norway succeeded in 1994 even though it did not complete the process, he says, while EU states Finland and Sweden secured special terms for agriculture in the far north.

But Eurosceptics doubt a carve-out is possible.

The head of the Icelandic Farmers' Association, Margrét Ágústa Sigurðardóttir, is unconvinced: "No member state has been granted a permanent opt-out."

She fears EU policies will focus on "the interests of 450 million consumers, rather than the specific needs of a country of 400,000 people".

When the BBC visited the airbase at Keflavik this month, fighter jets were taking off, and the Stars and Stripes was flapping alongside the Belgian tricolour and Nato flags.

With no military, Iceland's security relies on its Nato allies and a 1951 defence pact with the US.

However, Trump's repeated comments on taking over Greenland, and the risk of a weakened Nato alliance have added to Iceland's concerns.

Officials point to Russia's maritime activities in waters close to Iceland as the main security issue and in June Icelandic authorities said a Russian intelligence ship was tracked passing through Iceland's Exclusive Economic Zone.

There was disbelief among Icelanders when Trump mistakenly referred to their country four times in his speech at Davos, when he meant Greenland. The new US ambassador had to apologise when he joked that Iceland could become the 52nd US state.

The "special relationship" is unchanged, emphasises Daði Már Kristófersson. Yet, the finance minister believes "an additional pillar is important", and the government signed a defence partnership with the EU in March.

Yet geopolitics, perhaps surprisingly, has been largely absent from Iceland's public debate.

For Snærós Sindradóttir of the European Movement in Iceland that is frustrating.

The referendum is happening now "100% [because of] security matters", she says.

Giant red letters spelling "JA!", meaning yes, fill the windows at the group's campaign office.

The Yes camp says EU membership offers greater financial stability, while adopting the euro could curb the country's stubbornly high inflation.

Since breaking away from Denmark in 1944, Iceland has transformed from a poor island into one of Europe's most affluent nations.

But prices in Iceland were 84% higher than the EU average, according to analysis by the academic union Viska, and interest rates have climbed to 8%.

"We get higher salaries, and it goes straight to the cost of everything," Sindradottir complains. "It's like a dog chasing its own tail constantly."

In downtown Reykjavik it is the high cost of living and sovereignty that people care about most.

"The biggest problem right now is for the generation who are trying to buy their own housing," says Adolf Fridriksson, 62. "The mortgage rates are terrifying."

Meanwhile, Helga, 22, believes joining the EU will be too costly: "The fishing industry, and everything else, should be in our control."

Saturday's result is being watched closely across Europe.

If the Yes vote wins, Icelandic officials say talks with Brussels will take "months, not years", as 11 of the 35 areas of negotiation were already finalised when they were broken off.

Leaders are taking note in neighbouring Norway, a traditionally Eurosceptic country and a fellow member of the EEA. But support for joining the EU is growing there too.

Gaining a rich and stable new member in Iceland would be a welcome win for EU enlargement, says Hallgrímur Oddsson, head of the EU-Iceland think-tank European Currents.

"But a No vote could also be perceived as a loss."
